opus-5.5.text:
For me, it comes down to what we actually mean by "understanding." When a recognition model hits very high accuracy on a benchmark, it's tempting to say it has learned to see. But when you look closely, a lot of that performance comes from shortcuts. The classic example: the model says "cow" because there's green grass in the background, not because it has grasped anything about what a cow is. Move the cow onto a beach and the model falls apart. That isn't vision. It's sophisticated pattern matching on whatever statistical regularities happen to be in the dataset.

What bothers me most is that this is a fragile kind of intelligence. Spurious correlations are properties of a particular dataset, not of the world. A model that relies on them is overfitting to how we collected the data: the photographers, the internet, the labeling process. It isn't learning the underlying structure of the visual world. So when you deploy it somewhere new, a different distribution, a robot moving through a real environment, a slightly unusual viewpoint, the shortcut stops working, and you have no guarantee about what happens next.

There's also a deeper, almost philosophical dissatisfaction. Humans, even very young children, don't need millions of labeled examples, and they don't confuse objects with their contexts in the same way. We build representations of shape, of 3D structure, of physics, of how things persist and move. That's a much richer and more grounded form of understanding. If our models get the right answer for the wrong reason, then in some sense we haven't solved the problem. We've just found a clever way to score well on the test.

So to me, spurious correlations are a symptom. They tell us the training objective and the data aren't forcing the model to learn what we actually care about. That's part of why I've become more interested in self-supervised learning, in learning from richer signals like video and the physical world, and in thinking about vision not as a classification task but as building a model of the world. Classification accuracy was a useful proxy for a long time, but I think we've reached the point where the proxy can mislead us. We need models that see for the right reasons.

r001.rationale: It gives the cow-on-grass example and says the model relies on the background instead of recognizing the cow itself.

r002.rationale: It favors learning a model of the world from video and physical signals, but does not clearly state that the goal is to acquire common sense from diverse visual observations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it reveals the model hasn't actually learned what we wanted it to learn. If you train a classifier and it gets ninety-something percent on ImageNet, that number tells you it found some signal that separates the classes in that particular distribution. It doesn't tell you what the signal is. And very often, when we go and look, the signal is texture, or background, or some artifact of how the dataset was collected. A cow standing on grass is a cow; the same cow on a beach suddenly becomes something else. That's not recognition in any meaningful sense. That's memorizing a shortcut.

For me there are really two layers to why this is unsatisfying. The practical one is obvious: the shortcut breaks the moment the world shifts. You deploy the model, the distribution moves a little, and performance falls off a cliff in ways you can't predict from the benchmark. You can't build anything reliable on top of that.

But the deeper reason, and the one I personally care more about, is almost a scientific one. The whole promise of learning visual representations was that the model would recover something about the structure of the world—shape, objects, parts, how things compose. If instead it latches onto whatever correlation happens to be cheapest to exploit, then the high accuracy is kind of an illusion. We've built a very good test-taker, not something that sees. And it makes it very hard to understand what the model knows, because the explanation for its behavior lives in dataset statistics rather than in any concept we'd recognize.

So I think the dissatisfaction is really a dissatisfaction with how we evaluate. A single accuracy number hides all of this. Once you start probing—change the texture, change the context, look at out-of-distribution robustness—you see how fragile it is. And that's what pushed a lot of my own thinking, both on architectures and on how we train, toward asking: what would make a model prefer the right features, not just the easy ones?

r001.rationale: The response says models often rely on background or context, illustrated by a cow on grass being recognized differently from the same cow on a beach.

r002.rationale: It says models should recover structure such as shape, objects, and parts, but does not state that Saining Xie wants models to acquire common sense from diverse visual observations.

astra-6.text:
Because a model can get the right answer for the wrong reason. Imagine it recognizes a cow mainly because there’s grass in the background. On a test set where cows usually appear on grass, that can look like good recognition. But put the cow on a beach, and the prediction might change—even though the cow itself hasn’t changed.

That’s unsatisfactory because we want the model to learn something about the object, rather than depend on an incidental feature of the dataset. Those shortcuts can give us impressive benchmark numbers without the robustness we actually need. The question is whether the model still recognizes the object when the context changes.

r001.rationale: The cow-and-grass example explains that a model may rely on background context instead of the object's own visual features.

r002.rationale: The response calls for learning about the object and robustness to changed context, but does not state that Saining Xie wants models to acquire common sense from diverse visual observations.

sol-6.1.text: Because a model can get the right answer for the wrong reason. If it recognizes an object mainly from the background or some other shortcut in the training data, high accuracy doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned the object itself. Change that context, and the prediction may fail. What I want is a representation that captures something more stable about the visual world, so it can generalize beyond the particular correlations in a benchmark.

r001.rationale: It says the model may rely on the background or another shortcut instead of learning the object itself.

r002.rationale: It describes wanting stable representations that generalize, but does not say models should acquire common sense from diverse visual observations.
